messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Affective Expression: Crying, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time

Vignette:
As she sat in her small studio, surrounded by half-finished canvases and paint-splattered easels, 73-year-old widow Emily couldn't shake off the feeling of unease that had been following her for months. It was a sensation that had become all too familiar since the fire at the local art museum, where she had lost not only her studio but also several of her closest friends. Emily remembered the night vividly – the smell of smoke and burning paint, the sound of shattering glass, and the sight of flames engulfing the building. Her memories were like photographs, frozen in time, each one evoking a wave of intense guilt. She couldn't help but wonder if she could have done something to prevent the tragedy. As she navigated her daily routine, Emily found herself on edge, always listening for sounds that might indicate someone was entering her home. She would often wake up in the middle of the night, her heart racing, and struggle to fall back asleep. Her irritability had increased, and she would snap at anyone who got too close or asked too many questions. The smell of alcohol was particularly potent – it brought her right back to that fateful night, when she had stumbled out of the burning building, her clothes reeking of smoke and paint thinner. Emily avoided social gatherings where drinks were served, fearful of being transported back to that terrifying moment. Physical touch also made her uncomfortable; she would flinch if someone tried to hug or pat her on the shoulder. It was as if her body had become a minefield, each sensation triggering a memory or an emotion she couldn't bear to confront. Emily's artwork, once her solace and passion, now felt like a chore. She struggled to create anything meaningful, as if her muse had been extinguished by the fire. Her friends and family tried to be supportive, but Emily pushed them away, convinced that she would never be able to feel normal emotions again. Her days were filled with distractions – reading, watching TV, or taking long walks – all attempts to keep her mind occupied and suppress the thoughts that lingered just beneath the surface. She avoided news reports about fires or disasters, fearful of being reminded of that awful night. Despite her best efforts, Emily couldn't shake off the feeling that her life was no longer worth living. Her beliefs about the world had been shattered – she could no longer trust that bad things wouldn't happen to good people. As she sat in her studio, surrounded by the remnants of her former life, Emily felt lost and uncertain, unsure of how to rebuild or move forward. It was this sense of hopelessness that finally brought Emily to seek help. She wanted to learn how to manage her memories, how to quiet the guilt and anxiety that had become her constant companions. As she began therapy, Emily held onto a glimmer of hope – perhaps, just perhaps, she could find a way to heal and rediscover the joy in living.
